newsitem.title: SPAIN: OPINION-France vote bad for Spain - H.Lumholdt. [corrected 10:01 gmt]
newsitem.headline: OPINION-France vote bad for Spain - H.Lumholdt. [corrected 10:01 gmt]

text.p: (Corrects headline from "vote good for Spain" to "vote bad for Spain").
By Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist, Bank of America, Spain
As an investor it is becoming quite costly these days to be too orthodox in one's view of the necessities in European economic policy.
Markets took the German stance seriously when Finance Minister Waigel used to warn that only countries which showed a sustainable deficit reduction would be allowed access to EMU.
And of course we all remember when similar warnings by the Bundesbank used to move the markets. All this is long gone.
Germany got its Stability pact, a concession by its European partners which was seen as necessary to make it trust countries with a relatively recent improvement in public finances.

But since then, it has become clear that even the very bastion of fiscal discipline itself would be forced to implement "accounting adjustments" to reduce its deficit sufficiently for the purposes of monetary union.

Indeed with the news that a revaluation of Germany's gold reserves was being considered came near certainty that EMU matters more to the German government than a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria, despite earlier insistence to the contrary.
The Spanish and the Italian markets cheered, and rightly so.
If Germany was willing to go down this road, clearly there would be little to stop others from doing the same and the sustainability of deficit reduction in 1997 would be much less of a concern.
With this new backdrop it is possible to see the outcome of the first round of the French elections as quite positive for the Spanish markets.

Forget concerns that a much weakened centre-right government in France would lack the courage to finish the fiscal consolidation programme or that a government led by Socialist-Communist opposition would wish to discontinue it.

Focus instead on the insistence on the part of the French socialists that Italy and Spain participate in the first wave of EMU. And should the existing centre-right government in France be able to continue after the second round of elections on June 1, weakened or not, the elections will have been the last obstacle to EMU.

In many ways, the risk to this happy view derives not really from France but from Germany. The convergence criteria were introduced for a reason. EMU, its historical importance notwithstanding, is also an economic arrangment and Germany stands to potentially lose out on the monetary side while the rest of Europe stands to gain.
This at least is the conclusion if the yardstick is the kind of stability which most Germans would agree has served them well in the post-war period.

The Spanish and Italian markets are discounting that the criteria will be formally or informally dismissed in the political process: the Euro will be weak, but convergence towards it still means lower levels of interest for the two ex-high yielders.
Meanwhile, cross your fingers and hope that no one asks the German voters what they think, before it is too late.
(NOTE - The opinions expressed in this column represent those of the author only. They should not be seen as representing the views of Reuters).
